fragility

/fruh-JIL-ih-tee/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Fragility means the state of being easily broken or damaged, the quality of a delicate object or structure that must be handled with care.

The museum shipped the ancient glass vases in custom foam crates because of their extreme fragility.

Worked Example

The conservator turned the pages of the four-hundred-year-old atlas with a thin bone spatula, never with her fingers. Centuries of dryness had given the paper such fragility that a corner could crumble away at an ordinary touch.

The brittle, crumbling paper shows fragility in its most literal sense: the atlas is physically so delicate that ordinary handling could destroy it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

flimsiness: Flimsiness is weakness that comes from thin, insubstantial construction: a flimsy shelf was never sturdy to begin with. Fragility can belong to something finely and solidly made, like antique glass, that simply cannot survive rough handling. Flimsiness blames the build; fragility describes how easily damage happens.

frailty: Frailty is the bodily weakness of a living person, especially someone elderly or ill. Fragility belongs to objects and structures: glass, old paper, thin ice, things that break or crumble under small forces. You would speak of a patient's frailty but a vase's fragility.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

sturdiness: strength and solid construction

durability: the ability to withstand wear and rough use

Where it sits · how little force causes damage — delicacy → fragility → brittleness

delicacy vs. fragility: Delicacy suggests something fine that calls for gentle handling, while fragility means the object can actually break or be damaged with very little force.

brittleness vs. fragility: Fragility means something is easily damaged, but brittleness means it is so rigid that it shatters or snaps the instant it is bent or struck.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — fragil

Root — fragil: from Latin fragilis, easily broken, itself from frangere, to break

Suffix — -ity

Suffix — -ity: noun-forming ending: the state or quality of

Put it together

Put it together: Fragility is the adjective fragile, from Latin fragilis, 'easily broken,' plus the noun ending -ity, 'the state or quality of.' Both trace back to the Latin verb frangere, 'to break,' so fragility is literally 'the quality of being breakable.'

Use the root in a new word: fracture

Use the root in a new word: fracture: The X-ray showed a hairline fracture in the runner's foot, a 'break' straight from the same Latin root, frangere, that gives us fragility.

Word Choice

neutral

Fragility names the physical quality of objects and structures that break or crumble easily, as in the fragility of old glass, thin ice, or dried paper. The matching adjective is fragile, and frailty is the better word for the bodily weakness of a person.
